VBO:0000663.summary: Danish-Swedish Farmdog is a small, slightly rectangular farm dog long kept on both sides of the Øresund. Its short coat, compact body, and quick, alert carriage suit the jobs it filled around farms: catching rats, sounding the alarm, and accompanying people. Denmark and Sweden formally recognized it under its present name in 1987.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Danish-Swedish Farmdog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Denmark and Sweden, 1987 recognition, farm watchdog/ratter/companion roles, compact rectangular form, and late maturity.

VBO:0200003.summary: Affenpinscher is a small, rough-coated German pinscher whose dense facial furnishings frame an unmistakably monkey-like expression. It began as a house dog in southern Germany and became a compact companion, with a nearly square body and a brisk, self-possessed outline.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Affenpinscher
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives southern German house-dog origins, rough coat, compact square build, facial hair, and the 1879 and Dürer references.

VBO:0200003.interestingFact: Affenpinschers appear in breed records by 1879, and their ancestors appear in woodcuts by Albrecht Dürer.
VBO:0200003.historicalRoots: Southern German house dog and companion.

VBO:0200010.summary: Akita is a substantial Japanese spitz with erect ears, a curled tail, and a quiet, powerful outline. In the Akita region, medium-sized Matagi hunting dogs became the foundation for a larger breed; nineteenth-century crosses with Tosas and mastiffs changed its size before breeders worked to recover its spitz character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Akita
sources.evidence: The FCI Akita standard recounts Matagi roots, nineteenth-century crossing and restoration of spitz type, and describes body, ears, tail, and permitted colors.

VBO:0200010.interestingFact: Akita coats may be red fawn, sesame, brindle, or white.
VBO:0200010.historicalRoots: Japanese Matagi roots and later spitz restoration.

VBO:0200023.summary: Alpine Dachsbracke is a low, sturdy Austrian scenthound built to keep working over mountain ground in rough weather. Hunters use its nose to follow wounded deer and to pursue hare and fox. Short legs, heavy bone, a dense coat, and a long body help it maintain a trail through steep, broken terrain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Alpine Dachsbracke
sources.evidence: The FCI standard specifies Austrian origin, mountain tracking work, short-legged robust build, dense coat, and Rudolf’s 1881 and 1885 trips.

VBO:0200023.interestingFact: Crown Prince Rudolf took Alpine Dachsbracken on hunting trips to Turkey and Egypt in the 1880s.

VBO:0200046.summary: American Eskimo Dog is an American member of the spitz family, with a bright white or biscuit-cream double coat, pointed ears, and a plumed tail over its back. Developed from German Spitz stock in the United States, it comes in toy, miniature, and standard sizes while retaining the same crisp, compact outline.

sources.title: Official breed standard: American Eskimo Dog
sources.evidence: The UKC standard describes German Spitz ancestry, American development, the name change, three size varieties, white or biscuit-cream coat, ears, and tail.

VBO:0200046.interestingFact: The name “American Eskimo Dog” replaced “American Spitz” during the First World War era.
VBO:0200046.historicalRoots: American development from German Spitz dogs.

VBO:0200055.summary: American Staffordshire Terrier is a muscular American bull-type terrier whose strength is packed into a compact, agile frame. A broad head, short coat, and balanced proportions give it a strong silhouette. Its powerful body retains a free, easy movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: American Staffordshire Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives U.S. origin, muscular yet agile and graceful build, broad head, short coat, and preferred height ranges.

VBO:0200068.summary: Appenzeller Sennenhund is a nimble, tricolor Swiss farm dog once used to drive cattle and watch homesteads in the Appenzell region. Its almost square frame, close coat, and tightly curled tail create a very different silhouette from the heavier Swiss mountain dogs. The breed combines cattle work with an alert farmyard presence.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Appenzeller Sennenhund
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Swiss origin, cattle-driving and watch roles, tricolor nearly square build, curled tail, and the 1853 historical mention.

VBO:0200068.interestingFact: An Appenzell cattle dog was described in an 1853 book about Alpine animal life.

VBO:0200083.summary: The Aidi comes from Morocco’s Atlas Mountains, where pastoral families used it to defend tents, possessions, and flocks from predators. Its solid, mobile frame and thick, bushy coat suit a life exposed to mountain cold and strong sun. It is a guardian of the flock rather than a dog bred to move sheep from place to place.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Aidi (Atlas Mountain Dog)
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Morocco and Atlas pastoral communities; describes protection of tents and flocks, thick coat, and says the breed did not herd flocks in the European sense.

VBO:0200095.summary: Despite its name, the Australian Shepherd took its modern form on American farms and ranches. This medium-sized herding dog is slightly longer than tall, agile without looking slight, and known for a coat that can be blue merle, red merle, black, or red. Its working outline was shaped by stock work in the western United States.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Australian Shepherd
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies U.S. development, western ranch use, Basque shepherd association, proportions, coat colors, and farm-herding role.

VBO:0200095.interestingFact: The breed name reflects an association with Basque sheepherders who arrived in the United States from Australia.

VBO:0200100.summary: Austrian Black and Tan Hound is a long-bodied, supple scenthound with a sleek black coat set off by clear tan marks. Austrian hunters valued its voice and nose for pursuing hare and tracking wounded game, whether on flat country or steep mountain ground. Its lean, capable build keeps the emphasis on movement and endurance.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Austrian Black and Tan Hound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Austrian origin, hare and wounded-game work, mountain and flat-ground use, medium size, supple body, and black-and-tan markings.

VBO:0200100.interestingFact: The breed is also called Brandlbracke, a name used for the black-and-tan hound in Austria.
VBO:0200100.historicalRoots: Austrian scenthound for hare and wounded game.

VBO:0200118.summary: Barbado da Terceira is an Azorean cattle dog from Terceira Island, used to move livestock and to watch the farm. Its bearded face and abundant, slightly wavy coat give a shaggy profile to a strong, agile working build. The breed remains closely tied to a specific island landscape and its cattle-keeping traditions.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Barbado da Terceira
sources.evidence: The Portuguese Kennel Club identifies Terceira Island origin, cattle-driving and guard functions, and describes the bearded, abundant-coated working form.

VBO:0200118.historicalRoots: Terceira Island cattle and farm dog.

VBO:0200125.summary: Basset Fauve de Bretagne is a short-legged, wire-coated French hound with a warm fawn color and far more speed than its low outline might suggest. Descended from the larger Griffon Fauve de Bretagne, it was used for rabbit, hare, fox, and larger game. Its sturdy frame and weather-resistant coat belong to a dog bred for active scent work.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Basset Fauve de Bretagne
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Breton ancestry, game pursued, fawn wiry coat, low sturdy build, and regional-to-national history.

VBO:0200125.interestingFact: The breed spread beyond Brittany in the late twentieth century after a long period of strong regional popularity.
VBO:0200125.historicalRoots: Brittany scenthound descended from the Griffon Fauve.

VBO:0200134.summary: The Bearded Collie is a lean, long-coated sheepdog of Scotland and northern England, where it worked among flocks in rough weather. Hair falls around the muzzle to form the familiar beard. Beneath the shaggy outer coat is a light, active body built to move easily over open ground.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bearded Collie
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes Scottish and northern English sheep-herding roots, sixteenth-century records, lean active build, and long harsh coat with facial furnishings.

VBO:0200134.interestingFact: Scottish records mention dogs resembling the Bearded Collie as far back as the sixteenth century.

VBO:0200154.summary: Bergamasco Shepherd Dog grew around the sheep routes of Italy’s Alpine and pre-Alpine valleys, especially near Bergamo. Its famous coat forms broad, felted flocks over a square, muscular body, creating a weather shield for a dog used to drive and guard herds. The silhouette is rustic, but the underlying build is balanced and mobile.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bergamasco Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Bergamo-area transhumance, herd-driving and guarding, square build, and three hair types forming flocks.

VBO:0200154.interestingFact: The coat’s three hair textures gradually combine into flocks rather than forming ordinary round cords.
VBO:0200154.historicalRoots: Italian Alpine herd work and seasonal sheep movement.

VBO:0200163.summary: Bichon Frise is a small Franco-Belgian companion with a white, loose-curl coat and a soft, rounded outline. Its ancestors traveled from Italy into Renaissance France; later the little dog appeared in portraits of European courts before finding a broader popular audience. Beneath the cloudlike hair is a sturdy, compact body.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bichon Frise
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Franco-Belgian patronage, Italian-to-French Renaissance history, court portraiture, the barbichon etymology, and white curled coat.

VBO:0200163.interestingFact: The name “bichon” developed from “barbichon,” a comparison to a tiny Barbet.
VBO:0200163.historicalRoots: European companion dog with Renaissance court history.

VBO:0200175.summary: The Bloodhound is a large Belgian scenthound with loose skin, long low-set ears, and a solemn expression. It belongs to the Saint-Hubert hound tradition and was developed for following human scent over long distances. The folds and ears frame one of the most recognizable heads in the hound world, while the substantial body is built for sustained tracking.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bloodhound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Belgian Saint-Hubert history, human-scent tracking use, large substantial build, loose skin, and long low-set ears.

VBO:0200175.interestingFact: The breed is also known as Chien de Saint-Hubert, after the abbey associated with its history.

VBO:0200193.summary: Border Collie is a British sheepdog built for stamina and precise movement. Its body is slightly longer than tall, with enough substance for work and a smooth, efficient gait. Both rough and smooth coats occur in many colors, leaving the balanced working outline as a constant.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Border Collie
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies British sheepdog use, balanced outline, body proportions, smooth and rough coats, broad color range, and white-color limit.

VBO:0200193.historicalRoots: British sheepdog selected for stock work.

VBO:0200204.summary: Boston Terrier is an American companion dog with a short square muzzle, compact body, and neatly patterned white markings against black, brindle, or seal. Its close coat and naturally short tail give it an exceptionally clean outline. The broad-headed little dog moves freely on a well-balanced frame.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Boston Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard states U.S. origin, companion use, head and body form, short tail, permitted colors, white pattern, movement, and the meaning of seal.

VBO:0200204.interestingFact: “Seal” describes a coat that looks black until a reddish cast appears in sunlight.

VBO:0200214.summary: Boykin Spaniel was developed in South Carolina for hunting birds and waterfowl from small boats and swampy cover. Its medium, compact body, rich liver-to-chocolate coat, and feathered ears suit a dog expected to flush and retrieve on both land and water. That practical setting gives the breed its distinctive place among American spaniels.

sources.title: AKC Official Standard for the Boykin Spaniel
sources.evidence: The standard gives South Carolina origin, portable-boat hunting, medium build, brown coat, and flushing role.

sources.title: AKC Boykin Spaniel history
sources.evidence: AKC documents swamp and waterfowl hunting and South Carolina state-dog designation.

VBO:0200214.interestingFact: The Boykin Spaniel is the state dog of South Carolina.
VBO:0200214.historicalRoots: South Carolina waterfowl and upland hunting spaniel.

VBO:0200234.summary: Briard is a long-coated French sheepdog that combined driving livestock with guarding it. A flexible, muscular body sits beneath the shaggy coat, and double dewclaws mark the hind legs. Its history reaches the French lowlands, where “chien de Brie” entered print in the early nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Briard
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives French lowland herding and guard work, 1809 name reference, wartime roles, supple build, long coat, and double rear dewclaws.

VBO:0200234.interestingFact: French forces also used Briards during both world wars for duties that included carrying supplies and finding wounded soldiers.

VBO:0200258.summary: The Bulldog is a low, broad, smooth-coated British breed with heavy shoulders, a short muzzle, and a compact body. Its early history includes bull-baiting; after that practice ended in Britain, the breed shifted toward companionship and a shorter, squatter form. Sound movement and clear breathing remain essential to its build.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bulldog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes early bull-baiting, post-1835 change, broad compact form, movement and breathing safeguards, and 1630s naming.

VBO:0200258.interestingFact: The name “Bulldog” was in use by the 1630s.
VBO:0200258.historicalRoots: British bull-baiting history followed by companion breeding.

VBO:0200270.summary: Calupoh is a Mexican wolfdog breed with a tall, balanced frame, pricked ears, and a usually dark coat. Its organized modern breeding and companion role sit alongside an older Mexican cultural history of wolf-dog crosses. Archaeological finds from pre-Hispanic sites show the symbolic importance those animals held.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Calupoh
sources.evidence: The Mexican national standard describes the modern companion wolfdog, tall dark-coated form, and archaeological evidence of symbolic wolf-dog crosses.

VBO:0200270.historicalRoots: Modern Mexican wolfdog breed with pre-Hispanic cultural references.

VBO:0200274.summary: Canaan Dog is a square-built Middle Eastern dog with erect ears, a wedge head, and a curled tail. Its alert, spare frame suits a history of watch and security work. The breed carries the clear outline of a primitive-type dog, with a short to medium coat and economical movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Canaan Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Israel as origin, watch and security use, square medium body, erect ears, curled tail, primitive type, and color range.

VBO:0200274.historicalRoots: Middle Eastern watch and security dog.

VBO:0200304.summary: Caucasian Shepherd Dog is a very large, heavy-boned guardian associated with the Caucasus and the steppe regions of southern Russia. Its thick double coat, broad head, and strong frame reflect a history of watching property and livestock across harsh climates. Power combines with a deliberate, balanced movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Caucasian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Caucasian and southern Russian distribution, guard roles, massive build, double coat, climatic hardiness, and Soviet selection history.

VBO:0200304.interestingFact: An organized selection program for the breed began in the Soviet Union in the 1920s.

VBO:0200323.summary: Cesky Terrier is a Czech, short-legged terrier deliberately developed from Scottish and Sealyham Terrier stock for fox and badger hunting. Its long, silky coat is clipped into a distinctive soft outline, with drop ears and a body longer than tall. What looks refined in profile began as a practical search for a lighter working terrier.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Cesky Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard names Horák, 1949, the Scottish–Sealyham cross, fox and badger purpose, drop ears, rectangular body, and soft clipped coat.

VBO:0200323.interestingFact: František Horák began the breeding program in 1949 near Prague.

VBO:0200351.summary: Chinese Shar-Pei is a compact, square-bodied dog from southern China, recognized by its tiny ears, broad muzzle, and loose folds around the head and shoulders. Earlier dogs worked in hunting and watching around provinces bordering the South China Sea. Its harsh short coat gives the breed its sandpaper-like name and texture.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Chinese Shar-Pei
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies South China Sea origins, hunting and watch use, square body, wrinkles, small ears, muzzle, and harsh short coat.

sources.title: American Kennel Club Chinese Shar-Pei breed profile
sources.evidence: AKC gives the literal sand-skin translation of Shar-Pei and describes its harsh, sandpapery coat.

VBO:0200351.historicalRoots: Southern Chinese hunting and watch dog.

VBO:0200361.summary: Chow Chow is a compact Chinese spitz-type dog with a mane-like ruff, high curled tail, and characteristic blue-black tongue. Guard and hunting roles in China preceded its arrival in Europe around 1800. Its leonine coat surrounds a sturdy body capable of free movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Chow Chow
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Chinese guard and hunting history, arrival in other countries around 1800, leonine shape, tail, tongue, and movement safeguards.

VBO:0200366.summary: Clumber Spaniel is a broad, heavy British flushing spaniel known for a steady pace through cover rather than speed. Its long, low body, large head, and mostly white coat create a very different field silhouette from lighter spaniels. The breed’s English history is closely linked with Clumber Park in Nottinghamshire, though its earliest ancestry remains less certain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Clumber Spaniel
sources.evidence: The FCI standard cites Clumber Park, a possible French antecedent, heavy body, slower working pace, white coat, flushing role, and quiet scent work.

VBO:0200366.interestingFact: Clumbers often work quietly through cover, following scent with a notably strong nose.
VBO:0200366.historicalRoots: British flushing spaniel associated with Clumber Park.

VBO:0200402.summary: Czechoslovakian Wolfdog has a wolf-like outline rooted in a documented breeding program that began with German Shepherd Dog and Carpathian wolf crosses in 1955. The resulting working breed is long-legged and rectangular, with a dense gray coat and pale mask. Later selection established a consistent breed type.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Czechoslovakian Wolfdog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard details the 1955 crosses in Czechoslovakia, both mating directions, working purpose, rectangular build, gray coat, and light mask.

VBO:0200402.interestingFact: Both male-dog-to-female-wolf and male-wolf-to-female-dog matings were used in the original experiment.
VBO:0200402.historicalRoots: Czechoslovakian working breed founded in 1955 wolf-dog crosses.

VBO:0200447.summary: Dogo Guatemalteco is a powerful, white-coated Guatemalan molosser developed for protection, service, and companionship. Large Bull Terriers, Boxers, and Dalmatians contributed to its formation around the early twentieth century. Its broad head and muscular, balanced body carry that mixed working heritage.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Dogo Guatemalteco
sources.evidence: The Guatemalan canine association standard gives origin, early formation breeds, former name, use, white coat, and muscular head and body.

VBO:0200447.interestingFact: For much of the twentieth century the breed was known as the Guatemalan Bull Terrier.
VBO:0200447.historicalRoots: Guatemalan protection and service dog developed in the early twentieth century.

VBO:0200454.summary: Drever is Sweden’s low, long-bodied scenthound, developed after Westphalian Dachsbrackes arrived from Germany in the early twentieth century. Its short legs let it follow deer at a pace suited to hunters on foot, while a robust, muscular body stays capable across rough ground. It is a purposeful hunting hound with a distinctive low silhouette.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Drever
sources.evidence: The FCI standard traces Westphalian imports to 1910, deer-tracking use, short strong body, and adoption of the name Drever in 1947.

VBO:0200454.interestingFact: The Swedish breed name “Drever” was adopted in 1947.
VBO:0200454.historicalRoots: Swedish deer-tracking hound from Westphalian Dachsbracke stock.

VBO:0200486.summary: English Cocker Spaniel is a compact British flushing dog developed around woodcock hunting. Its hanging ears, softly feathered coat, and constant, busy movement belong to a dog made for searching heavy cover. The modern breed includes working and show lines, with the latter generally carrying a sturdier outline and more coat.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: English Cocker Spaniel
sources.evidence: The FCI standard explains woodcock naming, separation from Field and Springer spaniels, flushing role, compact build, and working/show distinction.

VBO:0200486.interestingFact: The word “cocker” comes from the woodcock the breed was used to flush.

VBO:0200497.summary: English Springer Spaniel is a leggy, compact British spaniel bred to find and spring game from cover. Before modern gun hunting, its work could send birds toward nets, falcons, or greyhounds; it later became a flushing and retrieving gun dog. Its balanced body and active gait distinguish it from lower, heavier spaniels.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: English Springer Spaniel
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes pre-gun springing work, present flushing and retrieving, compact athletic build, and comparative leg length.

VBO:0200497.interestingFact: The English Springer stands taller on its legs than the other British land spaniels.

VBO:0200509.summary: Estrela Mountain Dog comes from Portugal’s Serra da Estrela, where it guarded livestock moving between valley and high summer pasture. This substantial mountain dog has a brisk, sound gait and occurs in both long- and short-coated forms. Its broad, rustic frame served work across changing elevation and weather.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Estrela Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives the Estrela region, livestock guarding, seasonal ascent, two coat varieties, and large balanced build.

VBO:0200509.interestingFact: Traditional summer pasture in the Estrela Mountains can reach roughly 2,000 meters.

VBO:0200520.summary: Fila Brasileiro is a massive Brazilian mastiff developed for watch and protection work. Its long, rectangular body combines heavy bone with unexpected agility, and loose skin gives the face and neck a draped outline. A characteristic rolling, ambling gait adds another mark of its powerful movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Fila Brasileiro
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Brazilian origin, watch-dog use, rectangular molosser build, loose skin, agility, and characteristic gait.

VBO:0200529.summary: Formosan Mountain Dog, also known as Taiwan Dog, is a dry, athletic native dog of Taiwan’s central mountains. Its pricked ears, almond eyes, wedge head, and sickle tail form a spare hunting-dog profile. Local hunters kept dogs of this type, and a 1980 university survey documented the surviving population.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Formosan Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI Taiwan Dog standard identifies mountain hunting roots, wedge head, erect ears, sickle tail, medium build, and the 1980 university survey.

VBO:0200557.summary: Galgo Español is a Spanish sighthound shaped for pursuing hare across open fields. Its narrow head, deep chest, pronounced tuck-up, and exceptionally long tail make a lean, elastic outline; coats may be smooth or rough. Its history belongs to Iberian plains and coursing traditions, with speed carried through a light but sound frame.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Galgo Español
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Spain, open-field hare coursing, long narrow form, chest and tail, and two coat textures.

VBO:0200577.summary: German Shepherd Dog took shape in Germany as a versatile herding and service dog, selected for a strong, slightly elongated body and efficient ground-covering trot. Its erect ears, wedge-shaped head, and dense coat frame a workmanlike silhouette. Both stock coat and long stock coat occur.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: German Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes German breed organization, 1899 club founding, herding and service roles, proportions, trot, ears, and coat varieties.

VBO:0200577.interestingFact: The breed’s official German club, the Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde, was founded in 1899.

VBO:0200604.summary: Giant Schnauzer began in southern Germany as a cattle-driving dog before becoming a broader working breed. It carries the Schnauzer’s square frame, hard wiry coat, strong eyebrows, and beard on a much larger, more powerful body. Its sturdy outline still allows agile, efficient movement.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Giant Schnauzer
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives southern German cattle work, square powerful build, wiry coat and furnishings, 1913 registration, and 1925 working recognition.

VBO:0200604.interestingFact: The breed entered a stud book in 1913 and was formally recognized as a working dog in 1925.
VBO:0200604.historicalRoots: Southern German cattle driving and later utility work.

VBO:0200615.summary: Grand Basset Griffon Vendéen is a French, rough-coated scenthound with a long, low body and straight front legs. It was refined from larger Vendéen griffons to follow hare through scrub and bramble, with a voice that helps the hunter track its course. The “grand” distinguishes it from a smaller basset relative while preserving the basset’s low outline.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Grand Basset Griffon Vendeen
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes origin from larger griffons, Paul Dezamy’s hare-hunting selection, straight legs, low long body, rough coat, and voiced work.

VBO:0200615.interestingFact: Paul Dezamy helped fix the type around a size suitable for catching hare.
VBO:0200615.historicalRoots: Vendéen hare hound refined from larger griffons.

VBO:0200636.summary: Greenland Dog is a strong Arctic spitz selected for hauling sledges with endurance through severe cold. Its dense double coat, erect ears, and bushy tail protect a broad, hard-working body. Inuit transport work shaped the breed over generations, and its size varies within a functional range.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Greenland Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Inuit sledge-dog history, polar work, dense coat, erect ears, tail, and size flexibility.

VBO:0200662.summary: Havanese is a small companion dog developed in Cuba from Bichon-type dogs brought across the Atlantic from the western Mediterranean. Its body is sturdy and low, with a soft, abundant, often wavy coat and an elastic step. The breed became a familiar presence in Caribbean households.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Havanese
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies western Mediterranean ancestry, development in Cuba, companion use, low sturdy frame, soft wavy coat, and elastic movement.

VBO:0200662.historicalRoots: Mediterranean Bichon ancestry developed in Cuba.

VBO:0200674.summary: Hovawart is a German estate guardian whose name joins old words for farmyard and watcher. Breeders rebuilt the type from farm dogs beginning in 1922, using other large working breeds to stabilize it. The result is a powerful, slightly long-bodied dog with a flowing coat and a more athletic outline than its size first suggests.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Hovawart
sources.evidence: The FCI standard explains the name, 1922 reconstruction and crosses, estate-guardian roots, long coat, and powerful proportions.

VBO:0200674.interestingFact: The revival program used, among others, German Shepherd Dogs, Newfoundlands, and Leonbergers.
VBO:0200674.historicalRoots: German farm and estate guardian rebuilt in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200688.summary: Ibizan Hound comes from Spain’s Balearic Islands, where hunters used it chiefly for rabbits in rocky, brushy terrain. Its tall, narrow frame, immense upright ears, and light-footed movement form a striking Mediterranean outline. Scent and hearing help it find rabbits even in dense cover.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Ibizan Hound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Balearic origins, rabbit hunting by scent and hearing, pack behavior, tall narrow form, and pricked ears.

VBO:0200688.interestingFact: When one Ibizan Hound finds a rabbit, others may join it in a coordinated hunt.

VBO:0200696.summary: Indian Spitz is a spitz-family companion dog kept in India and shown under its own name at native-breed events. The breed occupies a familiar place in Indian households as well as the country’s organized dog-show world.

sources.title: Indian Veterinary Research Institute study of Indian Spitz dogs
sources.evidence: The 2019 original study identifies Indian Spitz as a spitz-family companion in India and reports a cohort of 24 owner-kept dogs.

sources.title: Andhra Pradesh Kennel Club 2017 show schedule
sources.evidence: The official schedule lists Indian Spitz by name within the Native Breeds show group.

VBO:0200706.summary: Irish Wolfhound is the tallest of the sighthounds: a rough-coated, powerfully made dog that still moves with long-legged grace. In Ireland it historically pursued wolves, deer, and wild boar, with wolf hunting continuing into the seventeenth century. Great scale and an active coursing build appear together.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Irish Wolfhound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Irish wolf, deer, and boar hunting, tall rough-coated sighthound form, movement, and the 391 written reference.

VBO:0200706.interestingFact: One of the earliest written accounts of Irish wolfhounds dates to 391 CE.

VBO:0200713.summary: Italian Greyhound is a small sighthound with a square, delicately made body, fine skin, and the long-legged proportions of a much larger coursing dog. Small hounds of this kind traveled through the Mediterranean into Italy, where the type flourished in Renaissance courts. Its slender limbs retain a running dog’s silhouette.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Italian Greyhound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes Mediterranean ancestry, arrival in Italy, Renaissance court prominence, square miniature-sighthound proportions, and fine coat.

VBO:0200713.interestingFact: Renaissance paintings frequently placed these small sighthounds beside nobles.
VBO:0200713.historicalRoots: Small Mediterranean sighthound developed in Italy.

VBO:0200732.summary: Jagdterrier is a compact German hunting terrier created after the First World War by breeders focused on field performance. Its dark, wiry or smooth coat and small, sturdy body suit work below ground as well as flushing above it. The breed has remained associated with a wide range of demanding hunting tasks.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Jagdterrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard recounts the postwar German breeding program, black-and-tan selection, underground and flushing work, and compact coat varieties.

VBO:0200732.interestingFact: The foundation program deliberately selected black-and-tan terriers for underground hunting.

VBO:0200740.summary: Japanese Spitz is a Japanese companion spitz with a pure-white standing coat, pointed muzzle, erect ears, and a plumed tail arched over the back. The breed emerged in the early twentieth century from white spitz dogs imported through several countries. Its small, well-balanced frame creates a crisp outline without the mass of a northern sledge dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Japanese Spitz
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Japanese development, early import history and 1921 exhibition, companion role, white coat, ears, tail, and proportions.

VBO:0200740.interestingFact: A white German Spitz imported via Siberia and northeast China was exhibited in Tokyo in 1921.
VBO:0200740.historicalRoots: Japanese white-spitz companion developed in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200749.summary: Kangal Dog is a large Turkish livestock guardian developed for protecting sheep across open country and harsh seasonal weather. Its short, dense coat, powerful rectangular frame, and dark facial mask are central to the breed’s look. Present-day work keeps it firmly tied to Turkish pastoral life.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Kangal Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Turkish sheep-guarding use, cultural context, dark mask, thick coat, powerful rectangular form, and caution about ancient origins.

VBO:0200758.summary: Karst Shepherd Dog is a Slovenian mountain guardian with an iron-gray, abundant coat and a robust but medium-sized frame. Written mention of the type appears in the late seventeenth century, while its traditional work centered on flocks in the Karst region. Its hanging ears and tail set it apart from erect-eared spitz herders.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Karst Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Karst origin, shepherd and guard use, iron-gray long coat, hanging ears and tail, and Valvasor’s 1689 reference.

VBO:0200758.interestingFact: Baron Janez Vajkart Valvasor mentioned the breed in a book published in 1689.
VBO:0200758.historicalRoots: Slovenian Karst flock and property guardian.

VBO:0200772.summary: Kintamani-Bali Dog is a native Indonesian spitz-type dog from the Kintamani highlands of Bali. A wedge head, pricked ears, sickle tail, and thick double coat form its mountain profile. Kept as a household companion around Sukawana, it comes from a region of volcanic slopes and forest.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Kintamani-Bali Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Sukawana/Kintamani origin, uncertain early history, household companion use, wedge head, ears, tail, and double coat.

VBO:0200779.summary: Komondor is a large Hungarian livestock guardian with a dense, corded white coat that can make its powerful frame almost disappear. Its roots are tied to pastoral life in the Carpathian Basin, where sheep and other stock needed protection. The cords are a defining working feature and develop as the coat matures, rather than being a decorative trim.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Komondor
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes Magyar pastoral roots, Hungarian herding tradition, large powerful build, and dense matted corded coat.

VBO:0200779.interestingFact: The Komondor’s ancestors are associated with Magyar pastoral movements into the Carpathian Basin.

VBO:0200808.summary: Lancashire Heeler is a short-legged, sturdy English cattle dog from the Ormskirk area, also historically used for rabbiting and ratting. Its compact frame, prick ears, and close black-and-tan or liver-and-tan coat carry a small dog’s version of working-cattle toughness. Its precise ancestry remains uncertain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Lancashire Heeler
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Lancashire/Ormskirk roots, cattle and vermin work, short sturdy build, coat colors, and uncertain Welsh-dog/terrier ancestry.

VBO:0200808.interestingFact: Its proposed ancestry includes Welsh cattle dogs and Manchester Terriers, though the exact history remains unproven.
VBO:0200808.historicalRoots: Lancashire cattle and farm vermin work.

VBO:0200819.summary: Leonberger is a giant German companion and watch dog developed near Stuttgart in the nineteenth century. Breeder Heinrich Essig used large breeds including Newfoundland, Saint Bernard-type, and Pyrenean Mountain Dog stock while seeking a lion-like presence. Beneath its heavy mane and feathering is a balanced, muscular dog meant to move freely.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Leonberger
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Essig’s nineteenth-century crosses, Leonberg origin, lion imagery, watch/companion role, mane, and balanced strong build.

VBO:0200819.interestingFact: The lion in Leonberg’s town crest helped inspire Essig’s desired appearance.
VBO:0200819.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century German giant companion and watchdog.

VBO:0200856.summary: Maltese is a tiny Mediterranean companion with a long, straight white coat that falls close to the ground. Small dogs of its type were kept around maritime settlements, and the exact origin behind the name remains uncertain. A long body and light, elegant carriage sit under the striking sheet of hair.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Maltese
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes maritime Mediterranean antecedents, uncertain name origin, tiny long-bodied form, white long coat, and companion role.

VBO:0200856.interestingFact: “Maltese” may draw on an old Semitic word associated with harbors, so the name does not establish a single island birthplace.

VBO:0200867.summary: Mastiff is a giant British guard dog with a broad, deep body and a massive square-looking head. Mastiff-type dogs were known in Britain for centuries, including before the fifteenth-century Battle of Agincourt. Its short coat and dark mask leave the powerful architectural shape in full view.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Mastiff
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives British history, watch use, giant square-headed structure, short coat and dark mask, and soundness requirement.

VBO:0200906.summary: Montenegrin Mountain Hound is a medium Balkan scenthound with a smooth black coat and sharply defined tan marks. Its solid, agile body served hunting in mountainous country, and the old name “black hound” reflects its most immediate visual feature. A written standard for the breed appeared in 1924.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Montenegrin Mountain Hound
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies Montenegro/Balkan hound roots, black-and-tan coloring, medium solid build, hunting role, old name, and 1924 standard.

VBO:0200930.summary: Neapolitan Mastiff is a massive Italian guard dog with a long, heavy body, deep folds, and a broad head. The breed survived around Naples and the foothills of Vesuvius for centuries. Its short coat and loose skin make the powerful southern Italian outline immediately recognizable.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Neapolitan Mastiff
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives southern Italian/Vesuvius history, Roman-mastiff tradition, guard use, massive long body, and loose skin.

VBO:0200945.summary: Norfolk Terrier is a tiny, sturdy terrier from the farm-dog traditions of East Anglia. It shares early roots with the Norwich Terrier but keeps its own silhouette through small folded ears. Low legs, a short back, and a harsh coat give this little dog the compact working form expected of a vermin hunter.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Norfolk Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard recounts shared East Anglian farm-dog roots with Norwich, low compact build, harsh coat, and dropped ears.

VBO:0200945.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200962.summary: Norwich Terrier is one of the smallest working terriers, a low, compact dog with upright ears and a wiry weatherproof coat. It emerged from the same East Anglian farm-dog background as the Norfolk Terrier, then became a distinct named breed. A short back and sturdy bone keep the lively outline grounded in practical vermin work.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Norwich Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives East Anglian shared history, small compact form, erect ears, harsh coat, and terrier background.

VBO:0200962.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200969.summary: Old English Sheepdog is a square, heavily coated British sheepdog whose gray-and-white jacket and rolling gait are hard to mistake. Beneath the weather-resistant coat is an able-bodied country worker with a topline that rises gently toward the rear. It has long carried the nickname “Bob-Tail.”

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Old English Sheepdog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives British sheepdog identity, Bob-Tail nickname, European ancestry hypothesis, profuse weatherproof coat, square body, and rolling gait.

VBO:0200969.interestingFact: Possible ancestors include European shepherd dogs mixed with British sheepdogs, though the exact lineage remains uncertain.
VBO:0200969.historicalRoots: British country sheepdog with mixed historical roots.

VBO:0200994.summary: Pekingese is a small Chinese companion with a broad head, flattened face, and lion-like coat around a low, compact body. Its heavy front end and flowing hair create a recognizable silhouette. The breed’s form still depends on free movement, clear breathing, and a coat that leaves the body’s shape visible.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pekingese
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Chinese origin, companion role, leonine appearance, broad head, low body, and safeguards for breathing, movement, and coat amount.

VBO:0201029.summary: Pointer is a British gun dog built to find game and mark its location with a still, directed stance. A strong yet supple body, deep chest, and clean, flowing curves give the breed both endurance and speed. Its short coat leaves the outline easy to read: this is a field athlete whose shape follows the work of scenting and pointing.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pointer
sources.evidence: The FCI standard identifies British pointing work, symmetrical curved outline, strong supple build, short coat, and endurance/speed.

VBO:0201043.summary: Pomeranian is the toy-sized German Spitz, carrying pointed ears, a foxlike head, an ample ruff, and a plume tail over the back in a very small frame. A dense undercoat holds the outer hair away from the body. The shared Spitz heritage is visible in every part of its crisp, alert outline.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pomeranian
sources.evidence: The FCI German Spitz standard names Toy Spitz/Pomeranian, German origin, watch and companion use, ruff, erect ears, tail, and standing double coat.

VBO:0201067.summary: Portuguese Podengo spans three sizes and both smooth and wire coats. Upright ears, a wedge-like head, and a sickle tail tie the varieties together, while different sizes traditionally pursued different game in Portugal’s varied terrain. Large, medium, and small dogs each preserve a distinct version of the same hunting heritage.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Portuguese Podengo
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Portuguese hunting and watch use, three sizes, two coats, ears, tail, and adaptations to terrain.

VBO:0201067.historicalRoots: Portuguese warren and other hunting traditions.

VBO:0201087.summary: Pudelpointer is a German rough-coated pointing dog founded from Poodle and Pointer stock, then developed as a distinct versatile gundog. Its sturdy, slightly long body and coarse protective jacket suit field, woodland, and water work. A beard and eyebrows frame a head built for nose-led hunting.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pudelpointer
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives German origin, Poodle–Pointer foundation, separate breeding, rough coat and facial furnishings, and all-round field/wood/water work.

VBO:0201087.interestingFact: The Poodle was used to create the foundation stock, but the breed was subsequently maintained apart from other pointing breeds.
VBO:0201087.historicalRoots: German versatile gundog from Poodle and Pointer stock.

VBO:0201109.summary: Pungsan Dog, also spelled Phungsan, is a Korean mountain hunting dog with a dense pale coat, upright ears, and a thick tail curled over the back. Its compact, muscular body and heavy coat suit the cold conditions of the northern peninsula. The breed also serves as a national symbol in the DPRK.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Pungsan Dog
sources.evidence: The university agricultural-college article identifies a Korean mountain hunting dog with pale dense coat, erect ears, curled tail, cold adaptation, and national-dog designation.

VBO:0201125.summary: Rat Terrier is an American farm terrier bred for controlling rats and other small vermin. Its smooth coat, sharply alert ears, and compact but athletic body suit quick turns in barns and fields. The breed comes in miniature and standard sizes, with a practical working outline that remains recognizable across both.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Rat Terrier
sources.evidence: The UKC Rat Terrier standard describes U.S. farm and vermin roots, athletic smooth-coated form, ear carriage, and two size divisions.

VBO:0201141.summary: Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog comes from the Carpathians, where large dogs were selected for flock work and guarding. A long, abundant coat covers the head, body, and legs, giving a sweeping outline to a strong, mobile dog. Males are typically taller and more powerful than females, with a clear difference in build.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Carpathian origins, herding and guarding roles, large long-coated form, and 1981 standard date; the Romanian breed name connects to sheep.

VBO:0201174.summary: Samoyed is a white Arctic spitz with an upcurved mouth, dark eyes, and a thick coat that forms the famous “Samoyed smile.” Dogs associated with northern Russian and Siberian peoples worked in reindeer herding, hunting, and sledding, often living close to their families. Beneath the bright coat is a medium-sized, endurance-oriented working shape.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Samoyed
sources.evidence: The FCI standard describes northern Russian/Siberian roots, reindeer, hunting and sled roles, living close to people, medium white spitz form, and the smile expression.

VBO:0201174.interestingFact: Northern Samoyed dogs lived so close to their people that they sometimes slept inside shelters for warmth.
VBO:0201174.historicalRoots: Northern Russian and Siberian sled and reindeer work.

VBO:0201184.summary: Schipperke is a small Belgian sheepdog-type companion and watcher with a wedge head, erect ears, and an all-black coat that rises into a dramatic neck ruff. It was already familiar in Flemish working neighborhoods in the seventeenth century. Strong, square, and fine-boned at once, it packs an unmistakable outline into a compact body.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Schipperke
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Belgian/Flemish roots, seventeenth-century working-class history, name etymology, watchdog use, wedge head, ears, and black ruff.

VBO:0201184.interestingFact: “Schipperke” comes from a Flemish expression meaning “little shepherd.”

VBO:0201198.summary: Scottish Terrier is a low, long-headed Highland terrier with short legs, a hard coat, and a powerful rear. The dark, sculptural profile has become famous, but the underlying breed was shaped as a tough ground-working terrier. A pronounced beard and eyebrows frame the head without changing its strong, narrow form.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Scottish Terrier
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Highland roots, 1882 club date, low powerful build, hard coat, long head, beard, and terrier work.

VBO:0201198.interestingFact: The Scottish Terrier Club formed in 1882, shortly after the first breed standard.

VBO:0201217.summary: Shetland Sheepdog is a small, long-coated sheepdog named for Scotland’s Shetland Islands. A refined wedge head, abundant mane, and agile movement give it a light working silhouette. Its dual history as sheepdog and companion is visible in a balanced frame under the profuse coat.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Shetland Sheepdog
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives British/Shetland identity, sheepdog and companion use, small graceful outline, wedge head, mane, and double coat.

VBO:0201217.interestingFact: Its coat includes a dense undercoat beneath long, straight outer hair.

VBO:0201233.summary: Siberian Husky is a medium northern sled dog built to carry light loads at moderate speed over great distances. A moderately compact frame, dense double coat, erect ears, and brush tail balance strength with quick, economical movement. It moves smoothly in harness and carries a lighter frame than many Arctic freight dogs.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Siberian Husky
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Siberian sled work, light-load long-distance performance, compact medium frame, coat, ears, brush tail, and efficient gait.

VBO:0201242.summary: Sloughi is a North African sighthound with a spare, long-legged body and a fine, short coat. It has lived across the region for centuries and remains strongly associated with Morocco. Lean muscle and a deep chest give it an elegant but unmistakably athletic outline.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Sloughi
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives North African history, Moroccan patronage, sighthound use, lean elegant body, and short-coat-only status.

VBO:0201242.interestingFact: The Sloughi occurs in a single, short-haired variety.

VBO:0201309.summary: Sussex Spaniel is a low, substantial British flushing dog with a rich golden-liver coat and a distinctive rolling movement. It was built to push through thick cover at a steady pace and to give voice while working, a useful signal when a hunter could not see the dog. Its solemn expression masks a field shape with strength and persistence.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Sussex Spaniel
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives flushing and voiced cover work, low strong form, golden-liver coat, and characteristic roll.

VBO:0201331.summary: Taigan is a Kyrgyz sighthound associated with high mountain hunting in Central Asia. Its tall, lean body carries a soft, long coat with feathering concentrated on the ears, legs, and tail; the face remains short-haired. Its proportions and coat suit coursing across broken upland terrain.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Taigan
sources.evidence: The German kennel federation’s national Taigan profile gives Kyrgyz origin, sighthound classification, coat and feathering, hunting use, dimensions, and national recognition status.

VBO:0201351.summary: Tibetan Mastiff, or Do Khyi, is a large Himalayan guardian historically associated with nomadic herders and Tibetan monasteries. Heavy bone, a broad head, and a dense coat with a neck mane give it a commanding mountain outline. Males may take at least four years to reach full maturity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Tibetan Mastiff
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Himalayan herder and monastery history, companion/watch/guard use, heavy coated form, mane, and slow maturity.

VBO:0201356.summary: Tornjak is a livestock guardian from the mountain districts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. Its nearly square, powerful body is covered by a long, thick coat, yet it remains an agile mover. Modern breeders rebuilt the breed from scattered surviving shepherd-dog stock after its numbers had become very low.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Tornjak
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Bosnian/Croatian mountain roots, livestock protection, near-square body, long coat, modern reconstruction, and medieval references.

VBO:0201356.interestingFact: Historical documents dated 1067 and 1374 mention dogs associated with the Tornjak’s region.
VBO:0201356.historicalRoots: Bosnian and Croatian mountain livestock protection.

VBO:0201389.summary: Vizsla is Hungary’s short-haired pointing and retrieving dog, recognizable by a lean frame and uniform russet-gold coat. It works through fields, forests, and water, with a nose and gait suited to locating and recovering game. Its ancestors accompanied Magyar movements into the Carpathian Basin, and Hungarian hunting records reach back centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Vizsla
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Magyar/Carpathian history, fourteenth-century records, field/forest/water gundog work, and russet-gold short coat.

VBO:0201389.interestingFact: Hungarian documents and illustrations depicting the type reach back to the fourteenth century.
VBO:0201389.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

VBO:0201411.summary: Welsh Springer Spaniel is a compact, enduring flushing dog with a vivid red-and-white coat. Its balanced, not overly leggy body was built for hard work through Welsh cover, with drive that shows in its brisk movement. Although related in purpose to other spaniels, the Welsh Springer keeps a distinct color and a longer, tapered head.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Welsh Springer Spaniel
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Welsh origin, flushing work, compact endurance build, red-and-white coat, head form, and energetic movement.

VBO:0201419.summary: Wetterhoun is a Frisian water dog from the northern Netherlands, historically used for otter and other small-predator hunting and to watch the yard. Its square, sturdy body and tightly curled coat fit work around Friesland’s lakes and waterways. The breed’s history is local and practical, with cart-pulling also recorded in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Wetterhoun
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Frisian origin, otter hunting and yard guarding, water-rich setting, cart work, square build, and curled coat.

VBO:0201419.historicalRoots: Frisian water hunting and farmyard work.

VBO:0201427.summary: Wirehaired Pointing Griffon is a rough-coated European gundog refined by Eduard Korthals in the nineteenth century. Its medium, slightly long body, square muzzle, beard, and eyebrows create a practical field silhouette. The versatile pointer can also follow the trail of wounded large game.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Wirehaired Pointing Griffon
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives Korthals history, versatile pointing and tracking roles, rough coat, rectangular body, square muzzle, beard, and brows.

VBO:0201442.summary: Yakutian Laika is a northern Russian sled and hunting dog developed by communities in the Sakha region. Its thick coat, erect ears, and strong but moderate frame suit travel and work in severe Arctic conditions. Regional references to sled and hunting dogs reach back centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Yakutian Laika
sources.evidence: The FCI standard gives northeast Russian aboriginal sled and hunting use, Arctic coat and build, and early regional written references.

VBO:0201442.interestingFact: Written references to dogs in the Yakutia region begin in the seventeenth century.
